h: The inner life of the soul and the holiness of Israel

p: "נַפְשִׁי יְשׁוֹבֵב יַנְחֵנִי בְמַעְגְּלֵי צֶדֶק לְמַעַן שְׁמוֹ",
"He restores my soul; He leads me in paths of righteousness for His Name's sake," (Psalms 23:3),
הוּא עַד דֻּגְמַת מַה שֶּׁנֶּאֱמַר: "וָאַעַשׂ לְמַעַן שְׁמִי לְבִלְתִּי הֵחֵל לְעֵינֵי הַגּוֹיִם",
this reflects that which is stated: "But I wrought for My Name's sake, that it should not be profaned in the sight of the nations," (Ezekiel 20:9),
כִּי כְּשֶׁיִּשְׂרָאֵל אֵינָם כָּרָאוּי נִתְחַלֵּל שְׁמוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ בֵּין הָאוּמּוֹת,
for when Israel do not conduct themselves properly, His Name, blessed be He, is desecrated among the nations,
כִּדְכְתִיב: "בֶּאֱמֹר לָהֶם עַם ה' אֵלֶּה וּמֵאַרְצוֹ יָצָאוּ",
as it is written: "In that men said of them: These are the people of Hashem, and are gone forth out of His land," (Ezekiel 36:20),
וְעַל זֶה נֶאֱמַר: "לָכֵן אֱמֹר לְבֵית יִשְׂרָאֵל: לֹא לְמַעַנְכֶם אֲנִי עֹשֶׂה בֵּית יִשְׂרָאֵל, כִּי אִם לְשֵׁם קָדְשִׁי וְגוֹמֵר",
and concerning this Scripture states: "Therefore say unto the house of Israel: Not for your sake do I this, O house of Israel, but for My holy Name, etc.," (Ezekiel 36:22),
וְכֵן הִתְפַּלֵּל דָּוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם: "לֹא לָנוּ כִּי לְשִׁמְךָ תֵּן כָּבוֹד וְגוֹמֵר",
and so King David, peace be upon him, prayed: "Not unto us, Hashem, not unto us, but unto Your Name give glory, etc.," (Psalms 115:1),
הַיְינוּ שֶׁלֹּא יִתְחַלֵּל שְׁמוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ, כִּדְכְתִיב: "לָמָּה יֹאמְרוּ הַגּוֹיִם אַיֵּה נָא אֱלֹהֵיהֶם".
meaning so that His Name, blessed be He, not be profaned, as written: "Why should the nations say: Where is now their God?" (Psalms 115:2).

paragraphs.text: Kisvei Rav Tzadok · Divrei Soferim 38:13: “But repair is complete when one merits complete repentance, so that deliberate sins become merits, to the point that through them he shall truly live, as stated in the chapter Yom HaKippurim (Yoma 86b). This comes through his heart burning like fire for the blessed God until all the dross and evil in the heart are consumed and it becomes wholly holy to God. It consequently becomes apparent that “all our deeds You have performed for us,” and that all the sins follow the pattern of “a transgression for the sake of Heaven,” which is greater than a mitzvah performed without that intention (Nazir 23b). From sins like scarlet there is made a scarlet garment of mitzvot. This is the defeat and destruction of the root of all evil and the power of the nations and Edom, as it is written: “Who is this coming from Edom, with crimson garments,” and so forth: He, as it were, wears Israel’s garment, made from their sins after they have been purified and shine like scarlet. This comes through Isaac, who says, “Half upon me and half upon You,” as stated in the chapter Rabbi Akiva (Shabbat 89b), unlike Abraham and Jacob, who said there, “Let them be erased for the sanctity of Your Name.” Our predecessors explained that this refers to the sins: let them be erased for the sanctity of the Name, so that if we have no merit, He will act for His great Name that is called upon us. This follows the verse, “Not for us … but to Your Name give honor … why should the nations say,” and so forth. Of this they said there, “Neither in the old man …”: this is still not counsel adequate to Israel’s merit. Although the sins will be erased as if they did not exist, what have they gained by being created and sent into this world?”

reviewedSourceExcerpt.he: אֲבָל שְׁלֵמוּת הַתִּקּוּן כְּשֶׁיִּזְכֶּה לִתְשׁוּבָה שְׁלֵימָה, שֶׁיִּהְיוּ זְדוֹנוֹת כִּזְכֻיּוֹת, עַד דַּעֲלֵיהֶם הוּא חַיֹּה יִחְיֶה, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּפֶרֶק יוֹם הַכִּפּוּרִים (יוֹמָא פ״ו עַמּוּד ב׳); וְזֶהוּ עַל יְדֵי שֶׁלְּבָבוֹ בּוֹעֵר כְּאֵשׁ לְהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ עַד שֶׁנִּשְׂרָף וְנִכְלָה כָּל הַפְּסֹלֶת וְהָרָע שֶׁבַּלֵּב וְנַעֲשָׂה כֻּלּוֹ קֹדֶשׁ לַה', מִמֵּילָא מִתְגַּלֶּה דְּגַם: "כָּל מַעֲשֵׂינוּ פָּעַלְתָּ לָּנוּ", וְכָל הַחֲטָאִים הוּא עַל דֶּרֶךְ "עֲבֵירָה לִשְׁמָהּ" דִּגְדוֹלָה מִמִּצְוָה שֶׁלֹּא לִשְׁמָהּ (נָזִיר כ״ג עַמּוּד ב׳), וְהַחֲטָאִים כַּשָּׁנִים נַעֲשָׂה מֵהֶם לְבוּשׁ שָׁנִים דְּמִצְוֹת, וּבָזֶה הוּא נִצּוּחַ וְאָבְדַן שֹׁרֶשׁ כָּל הָרַע וְכֹחַ הָאֻמּוֹת וֶאֱדוֹם; וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "מִי זֶה בָּא מֵאֱדוֹם חֲמוּץ בְּגָדִים וְגוֹמֵר", שֶׁכִּבְיָכוֹל לוֹבֵשׁ לְבוּשָׁן שֶׁל יִשְׂרָאֵל הַנַּעֲשֶׂה מֵחֲטָאֵיהֶם אַחַר שֶׁנִּזְדַּכְּכוּ וּמַזְהִירִים כַּשָּׁנִים. וְזֶהוּ עַל יְדֵי יִצְחָק שֶׁאוֹמֵר: "פַּלְגָא עָלַי וּפַלְגָא עָלָךְ", כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּפֶרֶק רַבִּי עֲקִיבָא (שַׁבָּת פ״ט עַמּוּד ב׳), וְלֹא כְּאַבְרָהָם וְיַעֲקֹב שֶׁאָמְרוּ שָׁם: "יִמָּחוּ עַל קְדֻשַּׁת שְׁמֶךָ"; וּפֵרְשׁוּ קַדְמוֹנֵינוּ דַּעֲוֹנוֹת קָאֵי, שֶׁיִּמָּחוּ בִּשְׁבִיל קְדֻשַּׁת הַשֵּׁם, שֶׁאִם אֵין לָנוּ זְכוּת יַעֲשֶׂה לְמַעַן שְׁמוֹ הַגָּדוֹל שֶׁנִּקְרָא עָלֵינוּ, וְעַל דֶּרֶךְ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: "לֹא לָנוּ וְגוֹמֵר כִּי לְשִׁמְךָ תֵּן כָּבוֹד וְגוֹמֵר לָמָּה יֹאמְרוּ הַגּוֹיִם וְגוֹמֵר"; וְעַל זֶה אָמְרוּ שָׁם: לָא בְּסָבָא וְכוּלֵי, דְּעַדַיִן אֵין זֶה עֵצָה הָרְאוּיָה לִזְכוּתָן שֶׁל יִשְׂרָאֵל, דְּהֲגַם שֶׁיִּמָּחוּ הָעֲוֹנוֹת וְיִהְיוּ כְּאִלּוּ אֵינָם, אַכַּתִּי מָה הוֹעִילוּ בְּמַה שֶּׁנִּבְרְאוּ וְנִשְׁלְחוּ לָעוֹלָם הַזֶּה;

sourceExcerpt.en: But repair is complete when one merits complete repentance, so that deliberate sins become merits, to the point that through them he shall truly live, as stated in the chapter Yom HaKippurim (Yoma 86b). This comes through his heart burning like fire for the blessed God until all the dross and evil in the heart are consumed and it becomes wholly holy to God. It consequently becomes apparent that “all our deeds You have performed for us,” and that all the sins follow the pattern of “a transgression for the sake of Heaven,” which is greater than a mitzvah performed without that intention (Nazir 23b). From sins like scarlet there is made a scarlet garment of mitzvot. This is the defeat and destruction of the root of all evil and the power of the nations and Edom, as it is written: “Who is this coming from Edom, with crimson garments,” and so forth: He, as it were, wears Israel’s garment, made from their sins after they have been purified and shine like scarlet. This comes through Isaac, who says, “Half upon me and half upon You,” as stated in the chapter Rabbi Akiva (Shabbat 89b), unlike Abraham and Jacob, who said there, “Let them be erased for the sanctity of Your Name.” Our predecessors explained that this refers to the sins: let them be erased for the sanctity of the Name, so that if we have no merit, He will act for His great Name that is called upon us. This follows the verse, “Not for us … but to Your Name give honor … why should the nations say,” and so forth. Of this they said there, “Neither in the old man …”: this is still not counsel adequate to Israel’s merit. Although the sins will be erased as if they did not exist, what have they gained by being created and sent into this world?

p: וְזֶה הוּא הַתְּפִלָּה גַּם כֵּן: "יַנְחֵנִי בְמַעְגְּלֵי צֶדֶק לְמַעַן שְׁמוֹ" –
And this is likewise the prayer: "He leads me in paths of righteousness for His Name's sake"—
שֶׁלֹּא יִתְחַלֵּל חַס וְשָׁלוֹם,
that His Name not be profaned, Heaven forbid;
יוֹלִיכֵנוּ בַּדֶּרֶךְ הָרָאוּי,
that He guide us along the fitting path,
כִּי כֹּל יָכוֹל ה', כָּל אֲשֶׁר חָפֵץ עָשָׂה.
for Hashem is omnipotent, doing whatever He pleases.
וְאַף עַכְשָׁיו אֵין עוֹד מִלְּבַדּוֹ,
And even now, there is none else beside Him,
וְאֵין כֹּחַ בְּשׁוּם נִבְרָא לַעֲשׂוֹת דָּבָר בְּלֹא רְצוֹנוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ,
and no created being possesses the power to perform anything without His divine will,
כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמַר יַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם: "הָאֱלֹהִים הָרֹעֶה אֹתִי מֵעוֹדִי",
as our father Yaakov, peace be upon him, said: "The God Who has been my shepherd all my life long," (Genesis 48:15),
וְדָוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם אָמַר: "ה' רֹעִי וְגוֹמֵר".
and King David, peace be upon him, proclaimed: "Hashem is my shepherd, etc." (Psalms 23:1).
רַק שֶׁעַכְשָׁיו אֵינוֹ בְּהִתְגַּלּוּת,
Only that in the present era it is not in overt manifestation,
וּלְעָתִיד יִהְיֶה בְּהִתְגַּלּוּת שֶׁכָּל הֶעָבָר נַעֲשָׂה רַק מֵרְצוֹנוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ.
whereas in the ultimate future it will be openly revealed that all of the past was enacted solely by His divine will.
וְעַל זֶה אָמְרוּ: "'אִם יִהְיוּ חֲטָאֵיכֶם כַּשָּׁנִים' – כַּשָּׁנִים הַלָּלוּ שֶׁסְּדוּרוֹת וּבָאוֹת מִשֵּׁשֶׁת יְמֵי בְרֵאשִׁית, כַּשֶּׁלֶג יַלְבִּינוּ" (שַׁבָּת פט עַמּוּד ב),

And concerning this they expounded: "'If your sins be as scarlet (kashanim)—like these solar years (kashanim) that are ordered and proceeding since the six days of Creation, they shall be white as snow' (Shabbat 89b),
כִּי הַכֹּל הָיָה מֵרְצוֹנוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ.
because everything was willed through His sovereign purpose.
וְזֶה שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: "גַּם כִּי אֵלֵךְ וְגוֹמֵר לֹא אִירָא רָע כִּי אַתָּה עִמָּדִי",
And this is what Scripture states: "Even though I walk, etc., I will fear no evil, for You are with me," (Psalms 23:4),
כִּי מִצַּד עַצְמֵנוּ אֵין כֹּחַ לַעֲשׂוֹת מְאוּמָה.
for from our own independent power we have no ability to accomplish anything.

This is “before whom they walked”: they walked with their own power. “But I—the God who has shepherded me from my beginning until this day”: in every particular act that I perform, I need the blessed God to open my eyes to what His will is. Even in an act in which I have already seen His will, if I am to repeat it, I must nevertheless see again, on the second occasion, what His blessed will is. In truth, in this respect Jacob was the greatest of the Patriarchs, for it is a great level that the blessed God should constantly guide a person. This was King David’s prayer, “The Lord is my shepherd; I shall not lack” (Psalms 23:1): may I never lack God’s providence over me, but may He constantly shepherd me, and may I also constantly recognize that He is my shepherd. For in His goodness the blessed God guides everything, but a person turns his face away and does not wish to look toward Him and pray. When a person prays a complete prayer, he is answered immediately and sees that the blessed God is the shepherd. This is “I shall not lack”: that I should not turn my face away from Him.”

reviewedSourceExcerpt.he: וַיֹּאמֶר הָאֱלֹקִים אֲשֶׁר הִתְהַלְּכוּ אֲבוֹתַי לְפָנָיו הָאֱלֹקִים הָרוֹעֶה אוֹתִי מֵעוֹדִי. הַיְינוּ שֶׁיַּעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ הָיָה מַקְטִין עַצְמוֹ נֶגֶד אֲבוֹתָיו אַבְרָהָם וְיִצְחָק, וְאָמַר כִּי לָהֶם הָיָה חָכְמָה וּבִינָה גְּדוֹלָה מְאֹד עַד כִּי הִרְחִיבוּ אֶת רְצוֹן הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מֵעַצְמָם, וְאַף אִם פָּתַח לָהֶם הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ פֶּתַח קָטָן, הָיוּ מַרְחִיבִים וּמִתְפַּשְּׁטִים אוֹתוֹ בְּחָכְמָתָם כְּדֵי לַעֲשׂוֹת רְצוֹן בּוֹרְאָם, וְהֵבִינוּ אַף בְּדָבָר שֶׁלֹּא הֵאִיר לָהֶם הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מְפֹרָשׁ, וְזֶה פֵּירוּשׁ "אֲשֶׁר הִתְהַלְּכוּ" הַיְינוּ שֶׁהָיוּ הוֹלְכִים בְּכֹחָם. אֲבָל אֲנִי, "הָאֱלֹקִים הָרוֹעֶה אוֹתִי מֵעוֹדִי עַד הַיּוֹם הַזֶּה", הַיְינוּ בְּכָל פְּרָט מַעֲשֶׂה שֶׁאֲנִי עוֹשֶׂה, אֲנִי צָרִיךְ שֶׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ יָאִיר עֵינַי אֵיךְ הוּא רְצוֹנוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ, וְאַף בְּזֶה הַמַּעֲשֶׂה שֶׁרָאִיתִי אֵיךְ הוּא רְצוֹנוֹ, אִם רְצוֹנוֹ לְשַׁנּוֹתָהּ, מִכָּל מָקוֹם צָרִיךְ אֲנִי לִרְאוֹת גַּם בַּפַּעַם הַשֵּׁנִית אֵיךְ הוּא רְצוֹנוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ, וּבֶאֱמֶת בְּזֶה הָעִנְיָן הָיָה יַעֲקֹב הַגָּדוֹל שֶׁבָּאָבוֹת כִּי זֹאת הִיא מַדְרֵגָה גְּדוֹלָה שֶׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מַנְהִיג אֶת הָאָדָם תָּמִיד, וְזֹאת הָיְתָה תְּפִלַּת דָּוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם (תְּהִלִּים כָּף גִּימֶל, אָלֶף) "הַשֵּׁם רוֹעִי לֹא אֶחְסָר", הַיְינוּ שֶׁלֹּא אַחְסִיר הַשְׁגָּחַת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ עָלַי וְרַק שֶׁיִּהְיֶה רוֹעֶה אוֹתִי תָּמִיד וְגַם אֲנִי אַכִּיר תָּמִיד שֶׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ הוּא רוֹעִי, כִּי הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ בְּטוּבוֹ מַנְהִיג כָּל דָּבָר, אַךְ שֶׁהָאָדָם מַחְזִיר פָּנָיו וְאֵינוֹ רוֹצֶה לְצַפּוֹת וּלְהִתְפַּלֵּל, וּבְעֵת שֶׁהָאָדָם יִתְפַּלֵּל תְּפִלָּה שְׁלֵימָה אָז תֵּיכֶף יֵעָנֶה, וְיִרְאֶה כִּי הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ הוּא הָרוֹעֶה וְזֶה פֵּירוּשׁ "לֹא אֶחְסָר" הַיְינוּ שֶׁלֹּא אַחְזִיר פָּנַי מִמֶּנּוּ.
reviewedSourceExcerpt.en: “He said: The God before whom my fathers walked, the God who has shepherded me from my beginning.” Jacob our father was making himself small before his fathers Abraham and Isaac. He said that they possessed very great wisdom and understanding, so that they expanded the expression of the blessed God’s will on their own: even if God opened a small opening for them, they broadened it through their wisdom in order to do their Creator’s will, understanding even something God had not explicitly illuminated for them. This is “before whom they walked”: they walked with their own power. “But I—the God who has shepherded me from my beginning until this day”: in every particular act that I perform, I need the blessed God to open my eyes to what His will is. Even in an act in which I have already seen His will, if I am to repeat it, I must nevertheless see again, on the second occasion, what His blessed will is. In truth, in this respect Jacob was the greatest of the Patriarchs, for it is a great level that the blessed God should constantly guide a person. This was King David’s prayer, “The Lord is my shepherd; I shall not lack” (Psalms 23:1): may I never lack God’s providence over me, but may He constantly shepherd me, and may I also constantly recognize that He is my shepherd. For in His goodness the blessed God guides everything, but a person turns his face away and does not wish to look toward Him and pray. When a person prays a complete prayer, he is answered immediately and sees that the blessed God is the shepherd. This is “I shall not lack”: that I should not turn my face away from Him.

p: וְאַחַר כָּךְ: "כִּי לְשִׁמְךָ תֵּן כָּבוֹד עַל חַסְדְּךָ עַל אֲמִתֶּךָ" –
And afterward: "For unto Your Name give glory, for Your kindness, for Your truth's sake" (Psalms 115:1)—
הַיְינוּ מִדַּת אַבְרָהָם וְיַעֲקֹב:
this points to the attributes of Avraham and Yaakov:
"חַסְדְּךָ" מְרַמֵּז לְמִדַּת אַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ שֶׁהָיָה מִדַּת חֶסֶד, הִתְפַּשְּׁטוּת הַקְּדֻשָּׁה;
'Your kindness' alludes to the attribute of Avraham our Father, whose trait was Chesed, the outward expansion of holiness;
וּמִדַּת יַעֲקֹב – "אֱמֶת לְיַעֲקֹב", חַיּוּת שֶׁאֵין לָהּ הֶפְסֵק, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמַרְנוּ.
and the attribute of Yaakov—'truth to Yaakov' (Micah 7:20), vitality that suffers no interruption, as we explained.
וְסִיֵּים הַכָּתוּב: "יִשְׂרָאֵל בְּטַח בַּה', עֶזְרָם וּמָגִנָּם הוּא וְגוֹמֵר",
And Scripture concludes: "O Israel, trust in Hashem; He is their help and their shield, etc.," (Psalms 115:9),
כִּי כְּפִי מַעֲלַת יִשְׂרָאֵל הֵם בּוֹטְחִים
for in accordance with the lofty stature of Israel, they trust
שֶׁאֲפִילּוּ עָבַר מַה שֶּׁעָבַר, וְ"גַם כִּי אֵלֵךְ וְגוֹמֵר" –
that even if all that transpired has occurred, and 'even though I walk, etc.'—
הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ עוֹזֵר לְהוֹצִיאָם וּלְהַצִּילָם,
Hashem, blessed be He, helps to extract and deliver them,
וּמָגֵן שֶׁלֹּא יוּכַל שׁוּם דָּבָר רַע לִפְגּוֹעַ בָּהֶם.
and shields them so that no evil thing can harm them.

h: The written and oral Torah and the Midrashic interpretation

p: וְהֵם שְׁנֵי עִנְיָנִים שֶׁבָּהֶם אָדָם נִיצּוֹל מִיֵּצֶר הָרָע:
And these represent two channels through which a person is delivered from the evil inclination:
"עֵזֶר" – עַד דֻּגְמַת מַה שֶּׁאָמְרוּ (סֻכָּה נב עַמּוּד ב):
'Help'—reflecting that which they taught (Sukkah 52b):
"יִצְרוֹ שֶׁל אָדָם מִתְגַּבֵּר עָלָיו בְּכָל יוֹם וְכוּלֵי, וְאִלְמָלֵא הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא שֶׁעוֹזְרוֹ אֵינוֹ יָכוֹל לוֹ";
'A man's inclination overpowers him every day, etc., and were it not that the Holy One helps him, he could not withstand it';
וּ"מָגֵן" הוּא מַה שֶּׁאָמְרוּ: "אִם פָּגַע בְּךָ מְנוּוָול זֶה – מָשְׁכֵהוּ לְבֵית הַמִּדְרָשׁ",
and 'Shield' is what they stated: 'If this vile one confronts you, drag him to the study hall,'
וְדִבְרֵי תוֹרָה נִקְרְאוּ "מָגֵן".
and words of Torah are designated as a shield.

paragraphs.text: Kisvei Rav Tzadok · Peri Tzadik, Vaetchanan 17:1: ““Every valley shall be lifted.” The root of the evil inclination is “Amalek, first of the nations,” the evil inclination of which it is said, “who cooled you”: it brings coldness and sadness into a person’s heart, making him slacken in Torah study because his deeds are improper and therefore his Torah and service supposedly accomplish nothing. We find this with Jabez: although through his reasoning he restored the Torah forgotten during the mourning for Moses, he nevertheless prayed, “‘That it should not grieve me’—that the evil inclination should not overpower me and prevent my study” (Temurah 16a). For this, the heart needs strengthening, as it is said, “His heart was lifted in the ways of the Lord”: one must believe that through one’s Torah one adds strength above, as it is said, “Give strength to God.” For this comes the promise, “Every valley shall be lifted.” “Every mountain and hill shall be lowered” means lowering the evil inclination, likened to a mountain, that introduces self-exaltation into the heart. “The crooked shall become straight” means straightening also the fool’s heart on the left, as it is said, “And joy for the upright of heart.” “The glory of the Lord shall be revealed, and all flesh shall see together that the mouth of the Lord has spoken”: it will become tangibly revealed that the voice calling within a person’s heart is truly God’s mouth, giving the power of awakening in his heart.”

הוּא יוֹם הַמִּיתָה, וְזֶה הוּא הַחִילּוּק שֶׁל יַרְגִּיז שֶׁגַּם כֵּן יִתְפָּרֵשׁ כְּעִנְיָן זֶה, אַךְ יַזְכִּיר לוֹ יוֹם הַמִּיתָה הַיְינוּ שֶׁיְּצַיֵּיר בְּמַחְשַׁבְתּוֹ כְּאִלּוּ עַתָּה זְמַן הַמִּיתָה וְאִם כֵּן אֵין לְהַחֶמְדָּה וְהַשִּׂמְחָה שׁוּם מָקוֹם, וּבְאִם אַחַר כָּל אֵלֶּה נִשְׁאַר עוֹד בְּלִבּוֹ הַחֶמְדָּה אוֹ הַשִּׂמְחָה, אָז רְאָיָה כִּי מֵהַשֵּׁם הִיא וְתִתְקַיֵּים לְעוֹלְמֵי עַד, וְכֵן הוּא הָעִנְיָן בְּיַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ בְּעֵת שֶׁשָּׁמַע הַבְּשׂוֹרָה כִּי עוֹד יוֹסֵף חַי שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר "וַתְּחִי רוּחַ יַעֲקֹב", וְהָיָה יָרֵא לְנַפְשׁוֹ פֶּן הַשִּׂמְחָה הַזֹּאת הִיא רַק שִׂמְחַת עוֹלָם הַזֶּה עַל כֵּן בָּחַן וְצֵירֵף אֶת עַצְמוֹ בְּאֵלּוּ הַבֵּרוּרִים, הַבֵּירֵר הָרִאשׁוֹן שֶׁאָמַר "אֵלְכָה וְאֶרְאֶנּוּ בְּטֶרֶם אָמוּת", הוּא נֶגֶד לְעוֹלָם יַרְגִּיז אָדָם כְּמוֹ שֶׁנִּתְבָּאֵר, וְהַשֵּׁנִי "וַיִּזְבַּח זְבָחִים לֵאלֹקֵי אָבִיו יִצְחָק", זֶה נֶגֶד יַעֲסוֹק בַּתּוֹרָה כְּעִנְיָן שֶׁמְּבָרְכִין בְּכָל יוֹם אֲשֶׁר קִדְּשָׁנוּ בְּמִצְוֹתָיו וְצִוָּנוּ לַעֲסוֹק בְּדִבְרֵי תּוֹרָה, כִּי הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא בִּנְתִינַת הַתּוֹרָה נִקְרָא גְּבוּרָה כָּךְ שָׁמַע מֹשֶׁה מִפִּי הַגְּבוּרָה (מְגִילָּה לָמֶד אָלֶף עַמּוּד בֵּית) כַּיָּדוּעַ לַמֵּבִין, וְשָׁם נֶאֱמַר לוֹ הַמַּאֲמָר "אָנֹכִי אַעַלְךָ גַם עָלֹה" אֲשֶׁר הוּא נֶגֶד הַמַּאֲמָר "אָנֹכִי הַשֵּׁם אֱלֹקֶיךָ אֲשֶׁר הוֹצֵאתִיךָ", רַק שָׁם הוּא לֶעָבָר וְהָכָא הוּא לֶעָתִיד, וְגַם מַה שֶּׁנֶּאֱמַר "וְאֶת יְהוּדָא שָׁלַח לְפָנָיו" וּפֵירְשׁוּ חֲכָמֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (מִדְרָשׁ תַּנְחוּמָא וַיִּגַּשׁ יוֹד אָלֶף) לְתַקֵּן לוֹ בֵּית תַּלְמוּד הָיָה גַּם כֵּן מֵעִנְיָן הַלָּזֶה, וְאַחַר כָּךְ בֵּירֵר בַּבֵּירֵר הַשְּׁלִישִׁי וַיֵּבְךְּ עַל צַוָּארָיו עוֹד וְדָרְשׁוּ חֲכָמֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה מְלַמֵּד שֶׁקָּרָא קְרִיאַת שְׁמַע, וְאַחַר כָּךְ אָמַר לְיוֹסֵף "אָמוּתָה הַפָּעַם" הוּא נֶגֶד עֵצָה הָרְבִיעִית יַזְכִּיר לוֹ יוֹם הַמִּיתָה, וּכְשֶׁרָאָה יַעֲקֹב כִּי אַחַר כָּל אֵלֶּה נִשְׁאַר לוֹ הַשִּׂמְחָה, אָז הֵבִין כִּי מֵהַשֵּׁם הוּא וְהוּא שִׂמְחָה אֲמִיתִּית וְקַיָּים לָעַד.
sourceExcerpt.en: “If he has overcome it [through Torah], well; if not, let him recite the Shema.” For in words of Torah there can be self-exaltation: through Torah a person can embolden himself, and this can prevent him from reaching true discernment. The counsel is therefore to recite the Shema. The meaning of Shema follows the Talmud’s teaching (Taanit 31a) that in the future the Holy One, blessed be He, will make a circle for the righteous: all will see that everything is in God’s hand and that no one has any superiority or exaltation over another. A circle is round and has no end; this is what the Shema alludes to. “If he has overcome it, well; if not, let him remind himself of the day of death.” He should picture in his mind that now is the day of death. This differs from “let him agitate [the good inclination],” which was also interpreted along these lines: here he should imagine that the time of death is now, so that the desire and joy have no place. If, after all these tests, the desire or joy still remains in his heart, this is evidence that it comes from God and will endure forever. So it was with Jacob our father when he heard the news that Joseph was still alive and “Jacob’s spirit revived.” He feared that this joy might be only worldly joy, and therefore examined and refined himself through these tests. The first, “I shall go and see him before I die,” corresponds to “let a person always agitate,” as explained. The second, “He offered sacrifices to the God of his father Isaac,” corresponds to engaging in Torah. We bless each day, “Who sanctified us with His commandments and commanded us to engage in words of Torah”; in giving the Torah God is called Might—Moses heard from the mouth of Might (Megillah 31b), as is known to one who understands. There he was told, “I shall also surely bring you up,” corresponding to “I am the Lord your God who brought you out”; the latter speaks of the past, and the former of the future. “He sent Judah ahead of him,” which the Sages explain as preparing a house of study (Tanchuma, Vayigash 11), also belongs to this matter. He then examined himself through the third test, “He wept on his neck further,” which the Sages interpret as teaching that he recited the Shema. Afterward he said to Joseph, “Now I can die,” corresponding to the fourth counsel, to remember the day of death. When Jacob saw that the joy remained after all these tests, he understood that it came from God: it was true joy, enduring forever.

paragraphs.text: Kisvei Rav Tzadok · Tzidkat HaTzadik 214:1: “Afterward: “May Your hand be with me” (I Chronicles 4:10)—that it should not be forgotten but remain in his possession. This is through “Your hand”: “your hand,” written with the extra letter heh, is interpreted as “the weak hand” (Menachot 37a), but “Your hand” here means the right hand. They said in Berakhot 6a, “At His right hand”—this is Torah, and so forth: God’s right hand imparts words of Torah. When it is with me, forgetting is impossible, for it continually imparts them. Because he asked for permanence, he immediately attached to this the request for companions, who maintain Torah in his possession, as explained above in paragraph 185. He placed the student before the companion because this was after the passing of Moses our teacher; see the Talmud there. Joshua had been appointed leader, occupied with allotting the land, and another occupation had begun. But Jabez—Othniel—had a heart trembling with desire for Torah; see there that he was sharper in reasoning than Joshua. He had neither companions nor students, so he first asked for blessing in Torah, since he was alone without teacher, companion, or student. Immediately with the blessing he had to ask for students, through whom he could become a vessel holding blessing. After the blessing he needed to ask for permanence and that he should not forget; then he asked for companions. Afterward, lest some sin interfere, he asked, “And keep me from evil, that it should not grieve me,” as our Sages explained there. Immediately, “God brought about what he asked.” Blessing, students, and companions could indeed come immediately in the plain sense. But permanence and protection from sin would apparently become known only at life’s end, when he saw that they had endured throughout his life. It seems that even this can be felt in the heart: when the words of Torah are fixed and enduring, he will not move from them, and transgression will not extinguish them, because there is enough in them to shatter the evil inclination. “Wisdom gives strength to the wise” (Ecclesiastes 7:19) and removes the fear that sin might interfere—the fear attributed to Jacob our father (Berakhot 4a). Someone whose strength comes from words of Torah is freed from every kind of fear.”

p: וְעֵזֶר הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ הוּא מַה שֶּׁמְּעוֹרְרָם לָשׁוּב עַל יְדֵי יִסּוּרִין,
And Hashem's assistance consists of awakening them to repent through tribulations,
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בַּזֹּהַר הַקָּדוֹשׁ (חֵלֶק ג, קסח עַמּוּד א):
and as written in the holy Zohar (III, 168a):
"אָעָא דְּלָא סָלֵיק בֵּיהּ נְהוֹרָא עַד דִּיבַטְּשִׁין בֵּיהּ, וּכְדֵין נָהֵיר",
'A piece of wood into which the fire does not catch until it is pounded, and then it burns bright,'
"כִּי אֶת אֲשֶׁר יֶאֱהַב ה' יוֹכִיחַ, וּכְאָב אֶת בֵּן יִרְצֶה",
"For whom Hashem loves He corrects, even as a father the son in whom he delights," (Proverbs 3:12),
וּכְתִיב: "כַּאֲשֶׁר יְיַסֵּר אִישׁ אֶת בְּנוֹ ה' אֱלֹהֶיךָ מְיַסְּרֶךָּ".
and it is written: "As a man chastens his son, so Hashem your God chastens you" (Deuteronomy 8:5).
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְנוּ כְּבָר בְּעִנְיַן שָׂכָר וְעוֹנֶשׁ,
And as we have already written concerning the matter of reward and punishment,
שֶׁהִקְשׁוּ: שֶׁבַּתּוֹרָה לֹא נִזְכַּר מֵעוֹלָם הַבָּא, רַק שָׂכָר וְעוֹנֶשׁ דְּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה;
where commentators questioned why the Torah does not explicitly mention the World to Come, recording only earthly reward and punishment;
שֶׁבֶּאֱמֶת, הַתּוֹרָה לֹא הִזְכִּירָה כְּלָל שָׂכָר וְעוֹנֶשׁ,
for in truth, the Torah did not intend to delineate ultimate reward and punishment at all,
וּמַה שֶּׁנֶּזְכַּר שָׂכָר וְעוֹנֶשׁ דְּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה אֵין זֶה שָׂכָר וְעוֹנֶשׁ,
and what is mentioned as earthly reward and punishment is not absolute retribution,
רַק סִיַּיעְתּוֹת מַה שֶּׁעוֹזֵר לַעֲבוֹדָתוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ:
rather divine assistances that facilitate His holy service:
"אִם בְּחֻקֹּתַי תֵּלֵכוּ... וְנָתַתִּי גִשְׁמֵיכֶם וְגוֹמֵר", וּשְׁאָר בְּרָכוֹת וְטוֹבוֹת,
“If you walk in My statutes... then I will give you rain in due season, etc.,” and all other blessings and benefits,
וְהֵם יְסַיְיעוּהוּ לַעֲבוֹדַת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ עַל יְדֵי הַרְחָבַת לִבּוֹ בְּטוֹבוֹת;
these serving to aid him in the service of Hashem by broadening his heart through prosperity;
וּבְאִם לָאו חַס וְשָׁלוֹם, יִהְיוּ הַסִּיַּיעְתָּא לְקִיּוּם מִצְווֹתָיו עַל יְדֵי הַהֵיפֶךְ חַס וְשָׁלוֹם;
and if not, Heaven forbid, the catalyst for observing His commandments will come through the opposite, Heaven forbid;
וְהַהֵיפֶךְ הוּא גַּם כֵּן לְעֵזֶר, שֶׁנּוּכַל לְהִתְגַּבֵּר וְלִכְבּוֹשׁ אֶת הַיֵּצֶר הָרָע.
and that opposite hardship is likewise an aid, empowering us to overcome and subdue the evil inclination.
וְזֶהוּ: "יִשְׂרָאֵל בְּטַח בַּה', עֶזְרָם וּמָגִנָּם הוּא".
And this is: "O Israel, trust in Hashem; He is their help and their shield."

paragraphs.text: Kisvei Ishbitz–Radzin · Tiferet Yosef, Bereshit 6: ““The Lord God said: It is not good for the human being to be alone.” My revered father explained: how could it apply to the blessed God that only now He saw it was not good for the human being to be alone, and did not see it before creation? Rather, this itself was a creation from God: the human being would find no help—that is, in his perception he would find no help. As my revered grandfather explained “I shall make him a helper opposite him”: within creation, every help comes from something that stands opposite. God placed every kind of obstacle before the person, and the person goes on expanding the honor of Heaven, removing the obstacles, and turning everything face to face toward God. Then he sees that all these obstacles supply assistance. Thus the Talmud says (Bava Metzia 84a) that originally, when Rabbi Yochanan stated a teaching, Resh Lakish would raise twenty-four objections [and Rabbi Yochanan would resolve them with twenty-four answers], and consequently the teaching became broader. God established that all assistance would come from something opposing. This is “If he merits, a help; if he does not merit, opposite him.” If he merits—if he overcomes and removes all those obstacles—he sees that he has every assistance: this is a help. Otherwise, God forbid, it remains opposite him.”

ביאר בזה כבוד אאמו"ר זללה"ה שמה שייך אצל השי"ת שרק עכשיו ראה שלא טוב היות אדם לבדו, ומקודם הבריאה לא ראה זאת. רק הענין בזה, דזה עצמו היה בריאה מן השי"ת שלאדם לא ימצא לו עזר, דהיינו שבתפיסתו בל ימצא לו עזר. וכמו שביאר בזה כבוד אזמו"ר זללה"ה אעשה לו עזר כנגדו, היינו אצל הבריאה הוא כל עזר מדבר שכנגדו, היינו שהציב השי"ת לאדם כל מיני מניעות והאדם הולך ומרחיב כבוד שמים ומסלק ממנו כל המניעות, ומחזיר את כל הדברים פנים בפנים להשי"ת, ואז רואה האדם שיש לו מן אלו המניעות כל הסיעתות. וכמו דאיתא בש"ס (בבא מציעא פ"ד.) מעיקרא כי הוה אמר ר' יוחנן מילי הוה מקשי ליה ריש לקיש עשרים וארבעה קושייתא [ומפרק ליה רבי יוחנן עשרים וארבעה פירוקי] וממילא רווחא שמעתא. והיינו שהציב השי"ת שכל הסיעתות לא יהיה רק מן דבר שכנגדו, וזה זכה עזר לא זכה כנגדו, זכה היינו אם מתגבר על כל אלו המניעות ומסלק ממנו, אז רואה שיש לו כל הסיעתות וזה עזר, ואם לא ח"ו אז כנגדו:
reviewedSourceExcerpt.en: “The Lord God said: It is not good for the human being to be alone.” My revered father explained: how could it apply to the blessed God that only now He saw it was not good for the human being to be alone, and did not see it before creation? Rather, this itself was a creation from God: the human being would find no help—that is, in his perception he would find no help. As my revered grandfather explained “I shall make him a helper opposite him”: within creation, every help comes from something that stands opposite. God placed every kind of obstacle before the person, and the person goes on expanding the honor of Heaven, removing the obstacles, and turning everything face to face toward God. Then he sees that all these obstacles supply assistance. Thus the Talmud says (Bava Metzia 84a) that originally, when Rabbi Yochanan stated a teaching, Resh Lakish would raise twenty-four objections [and Rabbi Yochanan would resolve them with twenty-four answers], and consequently the teaching became broader. God established that all assistance would come from something opposing. This is “If he merits, a help; if he does not merit, opposite him.” If he merits—if he overcomes and removes all those obstacles—he sees that he has every assistance: this is a help. Otherwise, God forbid, it remains opposite him.

h: Your rod and Your staff, they comfort me

p: וְזֶה שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: "שִׁבְטְךָ וּמִשְׁעַנְתֶּךָ הֵמָּה יְנַחֲמֻנִי",
And this is what Scripture states: "Your rod and Your staff, they comfort me," (Psalms 23:4),
כִּי "מִשְׁעַנְתֶּךָ" מְרַמֵּז עַל דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה,
for 'Your staff' alludes to words of Torah,
כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (חֲגִיגָה יד עַמּוּד א) עַל פָּסוּק: "מַשְׁעֵן וּמַשְׁעֵנָה, כֹּל מִשְׁעַן לֶחֶם וְכֹל מִשְׁעַן מָיִם" – הַכֹּל עַל דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה, עַיֵּין שָׁם;
as they expounded (Chagigah 14a) on the verse: 'the stay and the staff, the whole stay of bread, and the whole stay of water'—all referring to words of Torah, see there;
וְ"שִׁבְטְךָ" הַיְינוּ הָעֵזֶר עַל יְדֵי יִסּוּרִין.
and 'Your rod' points to assistance achieved through tribulations.
וְהִתְפַּלֵּל דָּוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם שֶׁיִּהְיֶה עַל יְדֵי יִסּוּרִין קַלִּים,
And King David, peace be upon him, prayed that this come through gentle afflictions,
כְּמַה שֶּׁנֶּאֱמַר: "יַסְּרֵנִי ה' אַךְ בְּמִשְׁפָּט",
as is stated: "O Hashem, correct me, but with judgment," (Jeremiah 10:24),
הַיְינוּ בְּרַחֲמִים, כְּאָב הַמְיַסֵּר אֶת בְּנוֹ שֶׁמֵּרִים הַשֵּׁבֶט עָלָיו וְאֵינוֹ מַכֵּהוּ, כְּרַחֵם אָב.
meaning with mercy, like a father disciplining his child who raises the rod over him yet does not strike him severely, in parental compassion.

paragraphs.text: Kisvei Rav Tzadok · Poked Akarim 2:5: “This occurred with Hannah, for Peninnah was given in her stead, as our Sages explained the verse “The barren woman has borne seven, and she who had many children languishes” (Midrash Shmuel 5; Rashi on I Samuel 2:5; Pesikta, section 44:7). It came through the great vexation with which her rival provoked her, in order to make her cry out. Although her intention was for the sake of Heaven (Bava Batra 16a), nevertheless “around Him it storms exceedingly” (Yevamot 121b): she had to bear punishment for causing Hannah momentary pain, even though it ultimately truly benefited her. This resembles stealing in order to repay double, which is forbidden (Bava Metzia 61b [editorial correction of the citation in the quoted Hebrew]). All His exacting treatment of the righteous and of the entire seed of Israel follows “as a man disciplines his son”: it comes from mercy, like a father’s compassion for his children or someone causing pain for the sake of healing. As it is said, “You alone have I known … therefore I shall attend to [your sins]” (Amos 3:2); it concludes with mercy, as explained in the first chapter of Avodah Zarah (4a). “I have known” is like “a kinsman of her husband,” meaning one who loves. Therefore “I shall attend”—through attention and providence, rather than withdrawing providence and handing them over to the way of nature, whose Hebrew numerical value is that of the name Elohim, through which the nations are judged. By contrast, of the children of Israel it is said, “For the Lord has afflicted her” (Lamentations 1:5), and in several places in Lamentations the name Havayah is used, for everything is in complete mercy.”

sourceExcerpt.en: This occurred with Hannah, for Peninnah was given in her stead, as our Sages explained the verse “The barren woman has borne seven, and she who had many children languishes” (Midrash Shmuel 5; Rashi on I Samuel 2:5; Pesikta, section 44:7). It came through the great vexation with which her rival provoked her, in order to make her cry out. Although her intention was for the sake of Heaven (Bava Batra 16a), nevertheless “around Him it storms exceedingly” (Yevamot 121b): she had to bear punishment for causing Hannah momentary pain, even though it ultimately truly benefited her. This resembles stealing in order to repay double, which is forbidden (Bava Metzia 61b [editorial correction of the citation in the quoted Hebrew]). All His exacting treatment of the righteous and of the entire seed of Israel follows “as a man disciplines his son”: it comes from mercy, like a father’s compassion for his children or someone causing pain for the sake of healing. As it is said, “You alone have I known … therefore I shall attend to [your sins]” (Amos 3:2); it concludes with mercy, as explained in the first chapter of Avodah Zarah (4a). “I have known” is like “a kinsman of her husband,” meaning one who loves. paragraphs.text: Kisvei Rav Tzadok · Resisei Layla 53:2: “This is the joy a person needs in his service, as it is written, “Serve the Lord with joy” (Psalms 100:2). Although he must also have fear—“rejoice with trembling”—this joy should never leave his sight either: he has merited to serve the blessed God. Is there any greater joy than this? The righteous act from love and also rejoice in afflictions (Shabbat 88b), because they recognize that everything comes from the blessed God, not from chance, God forbid. It is like a father who strikes his son to set him on the right path, or a physician who performs painful procedures on a patient to keep him alive. Although the patient is distressed now, he will certainly be glad afterward. One who understands and recognizes this even at the time is glad then as well.”

paragraphs.text: Kisvei Ishbitz–Radzin · Beit Yaakov on Torah, Chayei Sara 28:1: ““Let the young woman to whom I say, ‘Please lower your jug so that I may drink,’ and who says, ‘Drink, and I will also give your camels water’—let her be the one You have designated for Your servant Isaac.” The reason he established this sign for himself is that Isaac our father’s quality is might, and when the quality of might is clear, it is included within the quality of kindness. What appears to the eye as rage and anger in this quality resembles the teaching in Tanna de-Vei Eliyahu Rabbah, chapter 1: the blessed God acts with Israel like a father who says to his son, “I am a lion toward you; I am a bear toward you.” The father’s deeper intention in this anger is the son’s good, so that he will improve his way. Likewise, the blessed God’s intention is Israel’s good: to make awe shine in their hearts so that they follow His will. In truth, the blessed God is then filled with mercy toward Israel. But when the quality of might branches out into concealing garments, it can give rise to anger with furious cruelty, which is only evil. Thus Esau was born from Isaac; of him it is said, “Rescue my soul from the wicked man, Your sword” (Psalms 17:13). He himself does not recognize the root of the quality of might, which at its root is included within kindness. Because he does not recognize it, he has no share in it at all: he is the complete opposite of that quality’s root.”

reviewedSourceExcerpt.he: וְהָיָה הַנַּעֲרָה אֲשֶׁר אוֹמַר אֵלֶיהָ הַטִּי נָא כַּדֵּךְ וְאֶשְׁתֶּה וְאָמְרָה שְׁתֵה וְגַם גְּמַלֶּיךָ אַשְׁקֶה אוֹתָהּ הוֹכַחְתָּ לְעַבְדְּךָ לְיִצְחָק וְגוֹמֵר. הָעִנְיָן שֶׁעָשָׂה לְעַצְמוֹ אֶת זֶה הַסִּימָן, כִּי מִדַּת יִצְחָק אָבִינוּ הוּא מִדַּת הַגְּבוּרָה, וּמִדַּת הַגְּבוּרָה כְּשֶׁהִיא בִּבְהִירוּת הִיא כְּלוּלָה בְּמִדַּת הַחֶסֶד. וּמַה שֶּׁנִּרְאֶה לָעַיִן שֶׁמִּדַּת הַגְּבוּרָה הוּא רִתְחָא וְכַעַס, הוּא כְּעִנְיַן דְּאִיתָא בְּתָנָא דְבֵי אֵלִיָּהוּ רַבָּא (פֶּרֶק א׳) שֶׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מִתְנַהֵג עִם יִשְׂרָאֵל כְּמוֹ אָב שֶׁאוֹמֵר לִבְנוֹ אֲרִי אֲנִי עֲלֵיכֶם דּוֹב אֲנִי עֲלֵיכֶם, שֶׁעוֹמֶק כַּוָּונַת הָאָב בָּזֶה הַכַּעַס הוּא לְטוֹבַת הַבֵּן שֶׁעַל יְדֵי זֶה יֵיטִיב דַּרְכּוֹ, כֵּן הוּא כַּוָּונַת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ לְטוֹבַת יִשְׂרָאֵל לְהַזְרִיחַ יִרְאָה בְּלִבָּם שֶׁיִּמָּשְׁכוּ אַחַר רְצוֹן הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, וּבֶאֱמֶת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ הוּא אָז מָלֵא רַחֲמִים עַל יִשְׂרָאֵל. אָכֵן בְּהִסְתַּעֲפוּת מִדַּת גְּבוּרָה בִּלְבוּשִׁים מַסְתִּירִים, נִסְתַּעֵף מִמֶּנָּה מִדַּת כַּעַס בְּאַכְזְרִיּוּת חֵמָה, שֶׁהוּא רַק רַע, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁנּוֹלַד מִמֶּנּוּ עֵשָׂו, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר עָלָיו (תְּהִילִּים י״ז:י״ג) פַּלְּטָה נַפְשִׁי מֵרָשָׁע חַרְבֶּךָ, שֶׁהוּא עַצְמוֹ אֵינוֹ מַכִּיר הַשּׁוֹרֶשׁ מִמִּדַּת הַגְּבוּרָה, שֶׁבְּשָׁרְשָׁהּ הִיא כְּלוּלָה בְּחֶסֶד, וְהוּא אֵינוֹ מַכִּיר זֹאת וְאֵין לוֹ חֵלֶק כְּלָל בָּהּ, מִפְּנֵי שֶׁהוּא הַהֵיפֶךְ לְגַמְרֵי מִשּׁוֹרֶשׁ הַמִּדָּה.
reviewedSourceExcerpt.en: “Let the young woman to whom I say, ‘Please lower your jug so that I may drink,’ and who says, ‘Drink, and I will also give your camels water’—let her be the one You have designated for Your servant Isaac.” The reason he established this sign for himself is that Isaac our father’s quality is might, and when the quality of might is clear, it is included within the quality of kindness. What appears to the eye as rage and anger in this quality resembles the teaching in Tanna de-Vei Eliyahu Rabbah, chapter 1: the blessed God acts with Israel like a father who says to his son, “I am a lion toward you; I am a bear toward you.” The father’s deeper intention in this anger is the son’s good, so that he will improve his way. Likewise, the blessed God’s intention is Israel’s good: to make awe shine in their hearts so that they follow His will. In truth, the blessed God is then filled with mercy toward Israel. But when the quality of might branches out into concealing garments, it can give rise to anger with furious cruelty, which is only evil. Thus Esau was born from Isaac; of him it is said, “Rescue my soul from the wicked man, Your sword” (Psalms 17:13). He himself does not recognize the root of the quality of might, which at its root is included within kindness. Because he does not recognize it, he has no share in it at all: he is the complete opposite of that quality’s root.

paragraphs.text: Tanya, Likkutei Amarim 29:3–6: “This is the counsel offered in the holy Zohar, where the head of the academy in Gan Eden said: “Wood in which the light does not rise is struck,” and so forth; “a body in which the soul’s light does not rise is struck,” and so forth. “The soul’s light” means that the light of the soul and intellect does not shine sufficiently to rule over the body’s material coarseness. Although he intellectually understands and contemplates Hashem’s greatness, it does not take hold and become attached in his mind strongly enough to enable him to rule over the heart’s materiality, because of its materiality and coarseness. The cause is the arrogance of the kelipah, which raises itself above the light of the Divine soul’s holiness and conceals and darkens its light. It must therefore be struck down and humbled to the dust. This means setting fixed times to humble oneself, to be “despicable and rejected in his own eyes,” as it is written. A “broken heart” means “a broken spirit”: the sitra achara. In the beinonim, this is the person himself, since the vital soul that gives life to the body remains in its original strength in his heart; consequently, it is the person himself.”

reviewedSourceExcerpt.he: וְזֹאת הִיא עֵצָה הַיְּעוּצָה בַּזֹּהַר הַקָּדוֹשׁ, דְּאָמַר רַב מְתִיבְתָּא בְּגַן עֵדֶן: ״אָעָא דְּלָא סָלִיק בֵּיהּ נְהוֹרָא – מְבַטְּשִׁין לֵיהּ כוּ׳. גּוּפָא דְּלָא סָלִיק בֵּיהּ נְהוֹרָא דְנִשְׁמְתָא – מְבַטְּשִׁין לֵיהּ כוּ׳״. פֵּירוּשׁ ״נְהוֹרָא דְנִשְׁמְתָא״, שֶׁאוֹר הַנְּשָׁמָה וְהַשֵּׂכֶל אֵינוֹ מֵאִיר כָּל כָּךְ לִמְשׁוֹל עַל חוּמְרִיוּת שֶׁבַּגּוּף.  וְאַף שֶׁמֵּבִין וּמִתְבּוֹנֵן בְּשִׂכְלוֹ בִּגְדוּלַּת ה׳, אֵינוֹ נִתְפָּס וְנִדְבָּק בְּמוֹחוֹ כָּל כָּךְ שֶׁיּוּכַל לִמְשׁוֹל עַל חוּמְרִיּוּת הַלֵּב, מֵחֲמַת חוּמְרִיּוּתָן וְגַסּוּתָן. וְהַסִּיבָּה – הִיא גַסּוּת הַקְּלִיפָּה, שֶׁמַּגְבִּיהַּ עַצְמָהּ עַל אוֹר קְדוּשַּׁת נֶפֶשׁ הָאֱלֹהִית, וּמַסְתֶּרֶת וּמַחֲשִׁיכָה אוֹרָהּ. וְלָזֹאת, צָרִיךְ לְבַטְּשָׁהּ וּלְהַשְׁפִּילָהּ לֶעָפָר, דְּהַיְינוּ, לִקְבּוֹעַ עִתִּים לְהַשְׁפִּיל עַצְמוֹ, לִהְיוֹת ״נִבְזֶה בְעֵינָיו נִמְאָס״, כַּכָּתוּב, וְ״לֵב נִשְׁבָּר״ – ״רוּחַ נִשְׁבָּרָה״, הִיא הַסִּטְרָא אָחֳרָא, שֶׁהִיא הִיא הָאָדָם עַצְמוֹ בַּבֵּינוֹנִים, שֶׁנֶּפֶשׁ הַחִיּוּנִית הַמְחַיָּה הַגּוּף, הִיא בְּתָקְפָּהּ כְּתוֹלַדְתָּהּ בְּלִבּוֹ, נִמְצָא – הִיא הִיא הָאָדָם עַצְמוֹ.

Yet lest it enter one's mind, Heaven forbid,
מֵאַחַר שֶׁהַכֹּל הוּא מֵהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, יוּכַל לֵילֵךְ בְּדֶרֶךְ לִבּוֹ בְּלֹא שׁוּם הִשְׁתַּדְּלוּת,
that since everything is from Hashem, one may follow the inclination of his heart without any exertion,
וְיִסְמוֹךְ עַל עֵזֶר הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ כְּמַה שֶּׁנֶּאֱמַר "כִּי אַתָּה עִמָּדִי",
relying passively upon Hashem's help as stated 'for You are with me'—
עַל זֶה מְסַיֵּים בְּמִדְרַשׁ תַּנְחוּמָא:
concerning this the Midrash Tanchuma concludes:
שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: "אִמְרַת ה' צְרוּפָה, מָגֵן הוּא לְכָל הַחֹסִים בּוֹ",
as stated: "The word of Hashem is tried, He is a shield unto all them that take refuge in Him," (Psalms 18:31),

paragraphs.text: Kisvei Rav Tzadok · Resisei Layla 53:2: “This is the constant joy of a person of Israel in having been created a Jew and planted among God’s planting for glory, the seed of Jacob. It is a joy with no sadness alongside it: nothing interposes or prevents this joy at having merited a portion in the living God. Even if one has sunk wherever he has sunk and multiplied sins beyond measure, the attachment of his root to its source has still not been severed or cut off. That is impossible among the descendants of Jacob our father, whose bed was complete, and “none of the banished will remain banished from Him.” This follows King David’s words on behalf of the entire congregation at its deepest descent and lowliness: “Even when I walk in the valley of the shadow of death, I shall fear no evil, for You are with me” (Psalms 23:4). Even if one walks in the lowest level of the dark alleys of absorption in this world’s desires and vanities—empty imaginings that last only a moment and are called the “valley of the shadow of death”—no evil has occurred at all, since “You are with me,” even at the mouth of a burglar’s tunnel. If so, “He will make his paths straight.””

paragraphs.text: Kisvei Ishbitz–Radzin · Tiferet Yosef, Talmud Anthology, Taanit 11: “The meaning is that through the hope and expectation with which Israel constantly hopes and waits for redemption—may it come speedily in our days—it is counted to them as though they had saved themselves. In truth, the power to hope came to them through the redemption from Egypt. In the Egyptian exile concealment had become so overwhelming that no one in Israel had any expectation or desire for redemption. From the time the blessed God redeemed us, He planted this power in our hearts: henceforth each person of Israel would hope and wait for everlasting redemption. Thus “Who redeemed Israel” refers to the redemption from Egypt; “Who redeems Israel” refers to the future redemption, with which the blessed God is constantly occupied, through the power of hope He planted in our hearts so that we would hope and await it. We say, “He brought His people Israel out from among them to everlasting freedom”; yet how many exiles have passed over us since the redemption from Egypt, and we have still not been saved! But as explained, through the redemption from Egypt God fixed in Israel’s heart the power to hope, expect, and continually await the future redemption. This is “Who redeems Israel”: God is constantly occupied with that redemption through the hope in Israel’s heart. In this merit they will be redeemed, and the redemption will be called by their name. paragraphs.text: Kisvei Rav Tzadok · Tzidkat HaTzadik 64:1: “Sometimes a person clearly sees that the blessed God assists him and agrees with his actions. Nevertheless, this is not proof that his actions are truly upright. Of this it is said, “Who guides you on the way you go” (Isaiah 48:17), which our Sages interpret: “A person is led along the way he wishes to go” (Makkot 10b). It says “on the way”: in Proverbs this means the way of Torah, as I explained above in paragraph 48. For the blessed God assists only when, in the person’s own judgment, he is walking in the way of Torah. The proof learned from Balaam also follows Balaam’s own judgment, according to his side: this way was upright for him as he was; understand this. Consider Elijah: our Sages said (Sanhedrin 113a) that the withholding of rain was difficult before God. Nevertheless, He told Elijah, “Go … and hide,” and miraculously helped him conceal himself from Ahab. Had Ahab’s party found him, they would have compelled him to undo the decree, as happened afterward and as Jehoram did to Elisha. Of this it is said, “It is not in Heaven” (Deuteronomy 30:12): although God miraculously assisted Rabbi Eliezer in showing that the law agreed with him, the Sages did not rely upon that (Bava Metzia 59b). They considered that it was because he wished to go on that path. This was also Israel’s complaint, “You have caused the Lord’s people to die” (Numbers 17:6). Although they had seen the extraordinary miracle in the destruction of Korach’s company, they nevertheless reasoned that “it is not in Heaven”: one cannot rely on this to establish that the law agrees with Moses and Aaron against Korach and his company. Rather, you wished to go on this path, and your merit is great; therefore “you have caused,” and so forth.”

sourceExcerpt.en: Sometimes a person clearly sees that the blessed God assists him and agrees with his actions. Nevertheless, this is not proof that his actions are truly upright. Of this it is said, “Who guides you on the way you go” (Isaiah 48:17), which our Sages interpret: “A person is led along the way he wishes to go” (Makkot 10b). It says “on the way”: in Proverbs this means the way of Torah, as I explained above in paragraph 48. For the blessed God assists only when, in the person’s own judgment, he is walking in the way of Torah. The proof learned from Balaam also follows Balaam’s own judgment, according to his side: this way was upright for him as he was; understand this. Consider Elijah: our Sages said (Sanhedrin 113a) that the withholding of rain was difficult before God. Nevertheless, He told Elijah, “Go … and hide,” and miraculously helped him conceal himself from Ahab. Had Ahab’s party found him, they would have compelled him to undo the decree, as happened afterward and as Jehoram did to Elisha. Of this it is said, “It is not in Heaven” (Deuteronomy 30:12): although God miraculously assisted Rabbi Eliezer in showing that the law agreed with him, the Sages did not rely upon that (Bava Metzia 59b). They considered that it was because he wished to go on that path. This was also Israel’s complaint, “You have caused the Lord’s people to die” (Numbers 17:6). Although they had seen the extraordinary miracle in the destruction of Korach’s company, they nevertheless reasoned that “it is not in Heaven”: one cannot rely on this to establish that the law agrees with Moses and Aaron against Korach and his company. Rather, you wished to go on this path, and your merit is great; therefore “you have caused,” and so forth.

paragraphs.text: Kisvei Ishbitz–Radzin · Tiferet Yosef, Talmud Anthology, Pesachim 3: ““We do not suspect that a weasel may have dragged chametz from one house to another or from one place to another … for if so, there would be no end to the matter” (Pesachim 9a). Its meaning is as my revered grandfather, of blessed memory, said: if a person, on his own side, cleanses, purifies, and clarifies himself as far as his reach extends, the blessed God then testifies that he is always drawn after His will and is connected with the light of His will. Thus it is written concerning Abraham our father, “As for Me, behold, My covenant is with you … shall surely be circumcised” (Genesis 17). In truth the law is that “one who is circumcised shall circumcise”; how, then, did Abraham circumcise himself? And why did the blessed God say, “As for Me, behold, My covenant is with you,” before he circumcised himself? The meaning is that, because Abraham had refined himself as far as his reach extended, the blessed God consequently testified that he was refined, as though he were already circumcised, since it was not in his power to refine himself further. But someone who does not refine himself, on his own side, as far as his reach extends, and instead relies on the blessed God to clarify everything for him—the blessed God does not clarify him. This corresponds to the Talmud’s teaching (Pesachim 117b): in the blessing associated with the Shema one says “Who redeemed Israel,” and in the Amidah, “Who redeems Israel.” In the Shema one accepts the yoke of the kingdom of Heaven, and one who accepts that yoke has the yoke of government and worldly occupation removed from him. That is, the blessed God will clarify that he has no burden to bear. Therefore, with the Shema one says “Who redeemed Israel,” because this occurred at the redemption from Egypt, as we say, “He brought His people Israel out from among them to everlasting freedom.” In the Amidah one says “Who redeems Israel”: as a person comes to refine himself on his own side, he prays that the blessed God show him how, through his service, he will be redeemed from the other exiles. This is “We do not suspect that a weasel may have dragged … for there would be no end to the matter.” A person need not be concerned about that which has no end: there are places in which he cannot clarify himself, and he need not fear them, provided that, on his own side, he clarifies himself as far as his reach extends. In those places beyond his capacity to clarify himself, the blessed God will clarify him, because on his own side he has purified and clarified himself as far as a person can.”

reviewedSourceExcerpt.he: (ט.) אין חוששין שמא גיררה חולדה מבית לבית וממקום למקום וכו' דא"כ אין לדבר סוף. הענין בזה, כמו שאמר כבוד אזמו"ר זללה"ה, אם האדם מצידו מנקה ומטהר ומברר עצמו עד מקום שידו מגעת. אז השי"ת מעיד עליו שהוא נמשך תמיד אחר רצונו ית', ויש לו חיבור עם אור רצונו ית'. כמו שכתוב באאע"ה (בראשית י״ז:ד׳) אני הנה בריתי אתך וגו' המול ימול וגו', אף שבאמת הדין הוא המל ימול, ואיך מל אברהם אבינו את עצמו, ומה זה שאמר לו השי"ת אני הנה בריתי אתך קודם שמל עצמו. אך הענין הוא, כיון שאאע"ה בירר עצמו עד מקום שידו מגיע, ממילא העיד עליו השי"ת שהוא מבורר וכאילו הוא נימול, כיון שלא היה בידו לברר עצמו יותר. אבל מי שאינו מברר עצמו מצידו עד מקום שידו מגיע, אלא שהוא סומך את עצמו על השי"ת שיברר אותו על הכל, אז אין השי"ת מברר אותו. וכמו שאיתא בש"ס (פסחים קיז:) בקריאת שמע גאל ישראל ודצלותא גואל ישראל, כי בק"ש מקבל עליו עול מלכות שמים, ומי שהוא מקבל עליו עול מלכות שמים מעבירין ממנו עול מלכות ועול דרך ארץ, היינו שהשי"ת יברר אותו שאין לו שום סבלנות. וזה בק"ש גאל ישראל, כי זה היה בגאולת מצרים, כמו שאנו אומרים ויוצא את עמו ישראל מתוכם לחרות עולם. ודצלותא גואל ישראל, היינו כי זה מה שהאדם בא לברר עצמו מצידו מתפלל גואל ישראל, היינו שמתפלל שיראה לו השי"ת איך שע"י עבודתו יהיה נגאל משאר גלויות. וזה אין חוששין שמא גיררה חולדה כו' דא"כ אין לדבר סוף, היינו שאין לאדם לחוש מזה מה שאין לדבר סוף, היינו שיש מקומות שאין ביכולת האדם לברר עצמו אין לו לחוש על זה, כיון שמצידו מברר עצמו עד מקום שידו מגיע. ועל אלו המקומות שאין ביכולת האדם לברר עצמו, יברר אותו השי"ת, כיון שמצידו טיהר ובירר עצמו עד מקום שביכולת האדם לברר:

This is “We do not suspect that a weasel may have dragged … for there would be no end to the matter.” A person need not be concerned about that which has no end: there are places in which he cannot clarify himself, and he need not fear them, provided that, on his own side, he clarifies himself as far as his reach extends. In those places beyond his capacity to clarify himself, the blessed God will clarify him, because on his own side he has purified and clarified himself as far as a person can.
